seasoned: Carrots and onions are the textbook reciprocal pairing. Intercropping trials have measured real reductions in carrot fly where the two grow together. Plant in alternating rows with enough onion density for the scent-masking to register, and note the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large solid blocks.

This is mostly a good-neighbor, efficient-space pairing with a modest pest-repel bonus.

beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between onions and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.

Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick while onions send a narrow bulb down with little leafy spread, so they occupy different space and the lettuce fills in between onion rows. The onion scent offers a little aphid deterrence over the lettuce as a bonus. Treat it as a space-and-timing pairing first, mild pest help second.

beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as onions, and the strong onion smell is thought to bother some of their pests.

Their sulfur scent helps mask the cabbage family and deter its signature pests, cabbage loopers, worms, and root maggots, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with broccoli showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil sprouts onions next time.
seasoned: Note your sowing or set-out date and the first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's germination pace for next season.

beginner: The plant grows more and more upright leaves. This stage matters most for how big your onions get, because each leaf turns into a layer of the bulb later. The more healthy leaves the plant grows now, the bigger the onion can be, so you want steady, unbroken growth.
seasoned: The plant adds upright tubular leaves one after another. This is the stage that decides bulb size: each leaf becomes a bulb ring, so the number of leaves a plant builds before bulbing sets its size ceiling. You want vigorous, uninterrupted leaf growth, not a check from drought, weeds, or cold.

beginner: Help the plant grow lots of leaves now. Feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer, keep the soil evenly moist, and keep weeds out. Do most of the feeding early, while it is making leaves, because feeding too late leads to soft necks that do not store well.
seasoned: Push leaf growth: side-dress nitrogen, hold moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds. Front-load the feeding so the canopy is built before day length triggers bulbing; nitrogen applied late goes to soft necks instead of rings.

beginner: Count the leaves and note when you fed the plants. The number of leaves when bulbs start forming is a good clue to how big they will be.
seasoned: Track leaf count and feeding dates; counting leaves at bulbing start is the best in-season predictor of final bulb size.

beginner: Day length is how long the daylight lasts. When the days reach the right length for your kind of onion, the plant stops making new leaves and the bottom starts to swell into a bulb. This switch is set by how long the days are where you live, not by the calendar, so you cannot speed it up. The bulb forms using however many leaves the plant already grew.
seasoned: Once day length crosses your cultivar's threshold (long, intermediate, or short day per the variety you planted), the plant stops adding leaves and the base begins to thicken. This is the photoperiod switch: the trigger is day length, set by your latitude and the season, not the calendar date or anything you do. Bulbing starts on whatever leaf count the plant reached, which is why the leaf stage mattered.

beginner: You cannot make this happen faster, so just keep watering steadily as the bulb starts to form. If nothing swells, or it swells when the plants are still tiny, you probably planted the wrong type of onion for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.
seasoned: There is no action that moves this trigger; the work was done in the leaf stage. Keep moisture steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted the right day-length class for your latitude (a mismatch shows up now as no bulbing or premature bulbing).

beginner: Write down when the bulbs started to swell and how many leaves the plants had. Over time this shows whether your onion type suits where you live.
seasoned: Note the date bulbing visibly began and the leaf count at that point; over seasons this confirms whether your variety's day-length class fits your site.

beginner: The leaves stay green and standing up while the bulb gets bigger below them, and you start to see the tops of the bulbs at the soil surface. This is when onions put on most of their size, so keep the watering steady; letting them dry out now makes smaller onions.
seasoned: Tops stay green and upright while the bulb swells underneath and shoulders begin to show at the soil surface. This is the fast-fill window; steady, even moisture now translates directly into size, while any drought check costs you final bulb weight.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and stop adding nitrogen fertilizer, because feeding now leads to thick necks that do not store. Do not pile soil over the bulbs or bend the green tops down to hurry them, an old trick that actually makes onions smaller, since those leaves are still feeding the bulb.
seasoned: Hold even moisture through the swell and taper nitrogen off; late nitrogen now thickens necks and works against storage. Do not pull soil up over the bulbs or bend the tops to force them, an old trick that backfires because the standing leaves are still feeding the bulb.

beginner: Note when you stopped feeding and any times the bed dried out. Comparing that to your harvest size shows how steady the watering needs to be.
seasoned: Log when you stopped feeding and any dry spells; matching those against final size tells you how tight your moisture needs to be.

beginner: The necks get soft and the green tops flop over by themselves. When about half of them have fallen, it is time to harvest. seasoned: The neck softens and the tops fall over on their own; about half the tops down is the harvest cue. After lifting, the bulb is not storage-ready until it is cured: outer scales turn papery and the neck dries tight, which seals the bulb against rot.

beginner: On a dry day, loosen the soil and lift the onions, handling them carefully so they do not get bruised (bruised spots tend to rot). Then dry, or cure, them for two to four weeks somewhere warm, shaded, and breezy until the skins go papery and the necks dry shut. Each green leaf builds one bulb scale, so leaf count at the moment bulbing starts sets the ceiling on bulb size. What triggers bulbing is day length, not the calendar: a cultivar switches from making leaves to filling a bulb only once daylight crosses its threshold. That threshold is what splits onions into long-day (14 to 16 hours, such as Walla Walla), intermediate-day (12 to 14 hours, such as Super Star), and short-day (10 to 12 hours, such as Texas 1015Y) types, and it is why the right variety depends on your latitude. Grow a heavy-feeding, shallow-rooted plant in loose fertile soil, keep moisture steady so growth never stalls, then ease off water as the tops fall to begin curing.

beginner: Your onions are ready to dig when about half the tops have flopped over on their own and the necks feel soft. A simple test: gently pinch the neck just above the bulb. If it is stiff, wait; if it is soft and floppy, it is time. Pull them on a dry day, then dry (cure) them.
seasoned: Bulb onions are ready when about half the tops have naturally fallen over and the necks have begun to soften and dry. Pinch a neck to judge maturity: a stiff neck is immature, a soft, limber neck is ripe, and a collapsed neck means over-mature. Lift on a dry day, then cure.

beginner: Onions are unusual: they start making a bulb based on how long the days are, not on the calendar. Each kind of onion needs a certain number of daylight hours before it will switch from growing leaves to growing a bulb. That is why onions are sold by "day length" instead of by hardiness zone. There are three kinds. Long-day onions need very long summer days (14 to 16 hours) and grow best in the North. Short-day onions need only short days (10 to 12 hours) and grow best in the South, where they are planted in fall or winter. Intermediate onions need about 12 to 14 hours and grow well across the middle of the country. Pick the kind that matches where you live: a northern onion planted in the South may never make a bulb, and a southern onion planted in the North makes only a tiny one. Day length decides when the bulb forms, but it does not change when you plant, which still depends on frost and soil temperature.
seasoned: Onion is photoperiodic: a bulb forms only once day length crosses a cultivar-specific threshold, at which point the plant stops adding leaves and starts filling a bulb. Cultivars fall into three classes by that threshold, long-day at 14 to 16 hours, intermediate-day at 12 to 14 hours, and short-day at 10 to 12 hours, so the suitable class depends on your latitude. Long-day types fit northern latitudes (roughly above 38 to 39°N), where summer days run long enough that plants build a large leaf canopy before the trigger; short-day types fit southern latitudes (roughly below 35°N), where they are planted in fall or winter and bulb as days lengthen; intermediate types span the middle (roughly 32 to 42°N) and grow well across much of the country. Plant the wrong class and a long-day onion in the South may never bulb, while a short-day onion in the North bulbs too early on few leaves and stays small. Day length triggers bulbing only; it never moves your planting date, which stays anchored to frost and soil temperature.
